name: James M. Buchanan: Tennessee farm boy to Nobel laureate
scope: The biographical anchor for public choice's founding figure. T1: JAMES McGILL BUCHANAN was born OCTOBER 3 1919 on a small farm outside MURFREESBORO, TENNESSEE -- the grandson of a Reconstruction-era Tennessee governor of the same name. He was the first in his immediate family to attend college, walking each morning to Middle Tennessee State Teachers College and paying his way by milking dairy cows and living at home. T2: after Pearl Harbor, Buchanan served in the US NAVY on Admiral Nimitz's staff in Honolulu (1941-45). Using the GI BILL, he entered the UNIVERSITY OF CHICAGO for graduate school in 1945 -- a Southern rural Democrat who arrived, in his own words, 'a libertarian socialist' and left, six weeks after a course with FRANK KNIGHT, a market-order convert. T3: Buchanan earned his Chicago PhD in 1948 under Knight's supervision. He kept his Tennessee accent for the rest of his life -- Nobel journalists in 1986 noted the SOUTHERN DRAWL as one of the more surprising things about the man who had just remade political economy. T4: Buchanan taught at the University of Virginia (co-founding the Thomas Jefferson Center for Political Economy 1957 with G. Warren Nutter), Virginia Tech (where he built the CENTER FOR STUDY OF PUBLIC CHOICE with Gordon Tullock in 1969), and finally GEORGE MASON UNIVERSITY, where he moved the Center in 1983 and made GMU the world capital of public-choice research. T5: on OCTOBER 16 1986 the Royal Swedish Academy awarded Buchanan the NOBEL PRIZE IN ECONOMIC SCIENCES 'for his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for the theory of economic and political decision-making' -- the FIRST Nobel ever given to public choice. Buchanan died at 93 on JANUARY 9 2013. Further rungs: at the Nobel ceremony he insisted on presenting Knight's portrait alongside his own; his year-of-fellowship in Italy (1955-56, on a Fulbright with Rome's Luigi Einaudi) is credited with shaping his interest in fiscal constitutions.

name: The Calculus of Consent 1962
scope: The book that founded public choice as a discipline. T1: in 1962, JAMES BUCHANAN and GORDON TULLOCK published THE CALCULUS OF CONSENT: LOGICAL FOUNDATIONS OF CONSTITUTIONAL DEMOCRACY with the UNIVERSITY OF MICHIGAN PRESS. Both authors were then at the University of Virginia, where Buchanan had co-founded the Thomas Jefferson Center in 1957. T2: the book's core methodological move: apply STANDARD ECONOMIC REASONING (self-interest, marginal analysis, opportunity cost) to POLITICAL ACTORS -- voters, politicians, bureaucrats. Where welfare economics had assumed politicians were BENEVOLENT SOCIAL PLANNERS trying to maximize public welfare, Buchanan + Tullock treated them as ORDINARY HUMANS responding to incentives, just like consumers and firms in markets. T3: the book distinguished two levels of political decision: the CONSTITUTIONAL level (the rules of the game) and the POST-CONSTITUTIONAL level (choices made within the rules). Individuals behind a VEIL OF UNCERTAINTY about their future position would rationally consent to constitutional rules that limit majority power -- because they cannot know whether they will be in the majority or minority on future issues. T4: this distinction anticipates John Rawls's 1971 'veil of ignorance' by NINE YEARS. Where Rawls asked what redistributive rules people would choose behind a veil, Buchanan asked what CONSTITUTIONAL CONSTRAINTS they would choose -- the two men were reasoning in parallel from independent starting points. T5: the book explicitly attacked the DEMOCRATIC-ROMANCE view: the assumption that if a policy is chosen by majority vote it must reflect 'the will of the people.' Once you model voters, politicians, and bureaucrats as self-interested individuals, majority outcomes reflect not moral wisdom but the balance of interest-group pressure, logrolling, and rational ignorance. The book was the SEED that grew into forty years of public-choice research at Virginia, Virginia Tech, and George Mason. Further rungs: the book grew from Buchanan and Tullock's shared interest during Tullock's arrival at Virginia in 1958; it was funded in part by an early grant from the Ford Foundation; a 50th-anniversary edition appeared from Liberty Fund in 2004.

name: Politics without romance: Buchanan's Nobel-lecture phrase
scope: The three-word slogan that defines public choice. T1: 'POLITICS WITHOUT ROMANCE' is JAMES BUCHANAN'S phrase for what public choice does -- strip the ROMANTIC assumption that politicians and bureaucrats act from pure public spirit and instead treat them as ordinary humans responding to ordinary incentives. T2: Buchanan used the phrase as the title of a widely-cited 1979 lecture published as 'Politics Without Romance: A Sketch of Positive Public Choice Theory and Its Normative Implications' (Institut fuer Hoehere Studien Vienna). He returned to it in his Nobel-year writings after 1986. T3: the phrase is DIAGNOSTIC. Traditional welfare economics compared REAL markets (imperfect, with failures) to IDEALIZED government (perfect, benevolent, all-knowing) and concluded government should intervene. Buchanan pointed out that this compared apples to angels: if you compare REAL markets to REAL government (imperfect, self-interested, information-constrained), the case for intervention is far less obvious. T4: the reasoning move: whenever an advocate argues 'the market has failed, therefore government must act,' the public-choice critic asks WHAT REASON HAVE YOU to believe that GOVERNMENT will do BETTER, given the incentives facing the actual politicians and bureaucrats who would design and administer the intervention? Thomas Sowell would later condense the same move to 'COMPARED TO WHAT?' T5: this is why public choice is called the 'GOVERNMENT FAILURE' school -- not because it denies market failure exists, but because it insists that GOVERNMENT FAILURE is a real category too, produced by identifiable incentives (concentrated beneficiaries organizing, dispersed victims not organizing, regulators being captured, bureaucrats maximizing budgets). The choice is never MARKET-FAILURE vs PERFECT-GOVERNMENT; it is always market-failure vs government-failure. Further rungs: Buchanan credited the RUSSIAN emigre-economist Peter Bauer for coining the closely-related phrase 'romantic view of the state'; the 1979 lecture was later republished in the Liberty Fund Collected Works of James M. Buchanan.

name: Buchanan's 1986 Nobel Prize
scope: The prize that put public choice on the world map. T1: on OCTOBER 16 1986, the ROYAL SWEDISH ACADEMY OF SCIENCES announced that JAMES M. BUCHANAN of George Mason University would receive the NOBEL MEMORIAL PRIZE IN ECONOMIC SCIENCES for that year. He was the sole laureate -- the Committee did not share the prize. T2: the OFFICIAL CITATION read: 'for his development of the CONTRACTUAL and CONSTITUTIONAL BASES for the theory of economic and political decision-making.' The wording was carefully general -- the Committee wanted to name the analytical contribution rather than the political-methodology school-name 'public choice.' T3: the prize was CONTROVERSIAL within the economics profession. Many mainstream economists thought Buchanan's Virginia-school work sat outside their conception of what economics was. PAUL SAMUELSON reportedly grumbled that the award was for POLITICAL SCIENCE, not economics -- which, if true, was exactly the point Buchanan had been making since 1962: the artificial disciplinary wall between economic analysis of markets and economic analysis of politics was itself a mistake. T4: Buchanan's NOBEL LECTURE, delivered December 8 1986 in Stockholm, was titled 'THE CONSTITUTION OF ECONOMIC POLICY.' He argued that economic policy should be evaluated not by the outcomes of individual choices but by the RULES governing those choices -- the constitutional / post-constitutional distinction he and Tullock had drawn in 1962. T5: the 1986 Nobel was the FIRST awarded to public-choice theory. RONALD COASE won in 1991 (for transaction-cost economics that anchored Buchanan's institutional turn); DOUGLASS NORTH won in 1993 (for institutional economics); ELINOR OSTROM won in 2009 (for polycentric governance of the commons). All four laureates share a debt to the analytical move Buchanan pioneered -- taking institutions seriously as objects of economic analysis. Further rungs: the 1986 prize came with about $290,000 (kronor equivalent); Buchanan donated a substantial portion to the Center for Study of Public Choice at GMU; his colleague Gordon Tullock was widely expected to share future prizes but never won -- a persistent complaint among public-choice scholars.

name: Buchanan's constitutional political economy: rules vs outcomes
scope: The move that made Buchanan a constitutional economist, not just a critic. T1: JAMES BUCHANAN'S mature work is called CONSTITUTIONAL POLITICAL ECONOMY. The core idea: the RIGHT LEVEL for political-economic analysis is not the individual POLICY choice, but the RULES that govern how such choices are made. T2: the RULES-vs-OUTCOMES distinction: analyzing whether a particular tax rate should be 20% or 25% treats each policy as a separate battle. Analyzing whether the CONSTITUTIONAL RULE should require a supermajority to raise taxes moves the debate to a level where interest-group pressure operates differently. T3: Buchanan and GEOFFREY BRENNAN articulated this most fully in THE REASON OF RULES: CONSTITUTIONAL POLITICAL ECONOMY (Cambridge University Press 1985). The argument: constitutional constraints are chosen behind a VEIL OF UNCERTAINTY about future position -- and constraints agreed to at the constitutional level bind BOTH the majority AND the minority in ways particular policy debates cannot. T4: the reasoning move: an advocate proposes a spending program that seems locally attractive. The constitutional political economist asks: what RULES OF THE GAME made this program politically possible? Would we have consented to those rules if we had been uncertain whether we would be a net beneficiary or a net payer? The move relocates the debate from OUTCOMES to CONSTRAINTS. T5: applied to fiscal deficits: Buchanan + Richard Wagner (DEMOCRACY IN DEFICIT: THE POLITICAL LEGACY OF LORD KEYNES, 1977, Academic Press) argued that the OLD constitutional norm of BALANCED BUDGETS was a rule that had disciplined politicians for a century. Once Keynes's General Theory legitimized deliberate deficit spending, the norm dissolved -- and deficits ratcheted upward. The problem was not any particular deficit; it was the LOSS OF THE RULE. Further rungs: Brennan (Australian philosopher-economist) was Buchanan's most important later co-author; the Cambridge University Press 1985 volume is the standard reference for constitutional political economy.

name: Gordon Tullock: the lawyer who co-founded public choice
scope: The self-taught intellectual who never got a PhD but shaped a discipline. T1: GORDON TULLOCK was born FEBRUARY 13 1922 in ROCKFORD, ILLINOIS. He graduated from the UNIVERSITY OF CHICAGO with a law degree (JD) in 1947 -- and that was his HIGHEST DEGREE. Tullock never earned a PhD; he became one of the most cited economists of the twentieth century as a self-taught scholar. T2: after graduating, Tullock served in the US FOREIGN SERVICE from 1947 to 1956 -- postings in Tianjin (during the Communist takeover of China), Hong Kong, and Korea. Watching Chinese bureaucrats and diplomats maneuver taught him more about political incentives than any economics course could have. T3: at the University of Virginia from 1958, Tullock met JAMES BUCHANAN. Their 1962 collaboration THE CALCULUS OF CONSENT founded public choice as a discipline. Tullock founded the journal PUBLIC CHOICE (initially titled 'Papers on Non-Market Decision Making') in 1966 and edited it for thirty-plus years. T4: Tullock's own book THE POLITICS OF BUREAUCRACY (1965, Public Affairs Press) applied economic reasoning to how BUREAUCRATS actually behave -- promoting their own careers, expanding their agency's staff and budget, protecting their turf against rival agencies. It was the book William Niskanen built on for his 1971 Bureaucracy and Representative Government. T5: Tullock was famously idiosyncratic. He worked at George Mason from 1983 to 2008, kept a Reagan-era Confederate flag in his office for decades as a deliberate provocation, wrote 30+ books and 500+ articles, and expected to share every public-choice-related Nobel. He never won one. He died NOVEMBER 3 2014 in Des Moines, Iowa. When Buchanan won in 1986, Tullock reportedly quipped that being CO-AUTHOR of the Calculus of Consent apparently did not count. Further rungs: Tullock's book AUTOCRACY (1987) applied public-choice reasoning to dictators as self-interested actors; his 2004 SELECTED WORKS runs to ten volumes in the Liberty Fund edition.

name: Tullock's 1967 paper: rent-seeking as deadweight loss
scope: The paper that identified the biggest deadweight loss in political economy. T1: in 1967, GORDON TULLOCK published a nine-page paper in the WESTERN ECONOMIC JOURNAL (now Economic Inquiry) titled 'THE WELFARE COSTS OF TARIFFS, MONOPOLIES, AND THEFT.' Its argument would become the foundation of RENT-SEEKING theory. T2: standard microeconomics taught that monopoly caused a triangular DEADWEIGHT LOSS -- the value of trades that would happen at competitive prices but do not happen at monopoly prices. Tullock pointed out that this MASSIVELY UNDERSTATED the total social cost. T3: the missing piece: firms and individuals will SPEND REAL RESOURCES trying to CAPTURE the government-granted privilege that creates the monopoly rent. Lobbyists, campaign contributions, congressional testimony, expensive law-firm hours, marketing to regulators -- all of these ARE ECONOMIC INPUTS being used unproductively. The DEADWEIGHT LOSS is not just the triangle; it is the WHOLE RECTANGLE of resources burned in the competition for the privilege. T4: Tullock illustrated with THEFT: the cost of theft is not just what thieves steal (a transfer that leaves the total the same); the REAL cost is the resources people spend on locks, alarms, insurance, and security guards, AND the resources thieves spend on tools and time. The whole edifice of theft-prevention and theft-preparation is DEADWEIGHT LOSS -- effort with no productive output. T5: applied to POLITICS: every tariff, license, subsidy, and regulatory privilege attracts LOBBYING RESOURCES equal in expectation to the rent being sought. If a $1B tariff protection is on the table, up to $1B in lobbying, legal fees, and campaign spending will be burned to obtain it -- and if competing firms fight it, they will burn resources on the other side. The visible triangle is small; the resource-burn RECTANGLE is enormous. This is why rent-seeking is called the greatest deadweight loss in political economy. Further rungs: the paper was initially rejected by more prestigious journals; Anne Krueger's 1974 paper on Indian import licenses would formalize the concept and give 'rent-seeking' its modern name.

name: Anne Krueger 1974: rent-seeking gets its name
scope: The paper that gave rent-seeking its standard name and applied it to a real economy. T1: in JUNE 1974, ANNE OSBORN KRUEGER published 'THE POLITICAL ECONOMY OF THE RENT-SEEKING SOCIETY' in the AMERICAN ECONOMIC REVIEW (vol 64 issue 3). Krueger was then at the University of Minnesota; she would later serve as Chief Economist at the World Bank (1982-86) and First Deputy Managing Director of the IMF (2001-06). T2: the paper's CONCEPTUAL MOVE was to give TULLOCK'S 1967 argument a permanent name: RENT-SEEKING -- the pursuit of income by capturing government-granted privileges rather than by producing goods and services. Tullock had described the mechanism in 1967; Krueger's 1974 paper gave it the vocabulary the profession would use forever after. T3: her empirical case was INDIA. Firms that received a license to import (say) machinery could then sell that machinery at scarcity prices; the license itself was worth enormous rent. T4: firms therefore spent ENORMOUS RESOURCES chasing licenses -- hiring lobbyists, cultivating officials, making side payments, staffing whole departments dedicated to license-application. Her paper showed that a large fraction of measured 'economic activity' in state-led economies was NOT PRODUCTIVE at all -- it was resources burned chasing government-granted rents. name: George Stigler 1971: the theory of economic regulation
scope: The paper that turned regulatory capture from suspicion into theory. T1: GEORGE STIGLER (1911-1991) was the Chicago-school economist most associated with the ECONOMIC ANALYSIS OF REGULATION. He won the 1982 NOBEL PRIZE in economic sciences for his work on industrial structure and regulation. T2: in 1971 Stigler published 'THE THEORY OF ECONOMIC REGULATION' in the BELL JOURNAL OF ECONOMICS AND MANAGEMENT SCIENCE (vol 2 issue 1, Spring 1971). Its central thesis stunned an economics profession that had assumed regulation was aimed at protecting the public. T3: Stigler's THESIS: 'AS A RULE, REGULATION IS ACQUIRED BY THE INDUSTRY AND IS DESIGNED AND OPERATED PRIMARILY FOR ITS BENEFIT.' Regulation was not IMPOSED on unwilling industries by public-spirited legislators; it was DEMANDED by industries themselves as a way to raise BARRIERS TO ENTRY against would-be competitors. T4: the mechanism: industries have a CONCENTRATED interest in favorable regulation; consumers have a DISPERSED interest that is not worth organizing around. Politicians facing a small group of intensely-interested lobbyists with money on one side and a large group of mildly-uninterested consumers on the other predictably favor the concentrated side. What LOOKS LIKE public-interest regulation is USUALLY captured-by-the-regulated-industry regulation. T5: Stigler tested the theory empirically -- looking at OCCUPATIONAL LICENSING (barbers, morticians, accountants all lobby to require licenses that RESTRICT ENTRY and raise incumbents' incomes), TRUCKING REGULATION (the ICC set rates that benefited existing trucking firms at the expense of consumers), and ELECTRICITY REGULATION (state utility commissions consistently favored the utilities they regulated). The pattern was the same across sectors: REGULATION is a PRODUCT that industries DEMAND and government SUPPLIES. Further rungs: Sam Peltzman formalized the model further in 'Toward a More General Theory of Regulation' (Journal of Law and Economics 1976); the 1978 airline deregulation and 1980 trucking deregulation were direct policy responses to this line of research.

name: Regulatory capture case studies: ICC, CAB, FCC
scope: The empirical evidence that turned Stigler's theory into a policy consensus. T1: the INTERSTATE COMMERCE COMMISSION (ICC) was created in 1887 to regulate the railroads, which shippers accused of monopoly pricing. Within a generation, historian Gabriel Kolko (THE TRIUMPH OF CONSERVATISM 1963) documented that the RAILROADS THEMSELVES had lobbied to create the ICC -- to stabilize rates and prevent price-cutting competition. T2: the CIVIL AERONAUTICS BOARD (CAB) was created in 1938 to regulate commercial airlines. For four decades it set airline routes and fares, and NEVER allowed a new trunk-line airline to enter the market. Airlines LOVED this -- guaranteed routes, guaranteed fares, no new competitors. In 1978 the AIRLINE DEREGULATION ACT (championed by economist ALFRED KAHN as CAB chairman under President Carter) broke the system. Real airfares FELL DRAMATICALLY over the next two decades. T3: the FEDERAL COMMUNICATIONS COMMISSION (FCC) was created in 1934 to regulate broadcast spectrum. Once the FCC granted broadcast licenses, those licenses became WORTH MILLIONS of dollars. License holders lobbied fiercely to prevent competing licenses being issued and to block new technologies (cable TV was delayed for years by broadcaster opposition mediated through the FCC). T4: the FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION (FDA) shows a DIFFERENT capture pattern -- the REVOLVING DOOR. Senior FDA officials routinely leave the agency for lucrative positions at pharmaceutical companies they had previously regulated. name: Mancur Olson: The Logic of Collective Action 1965
scope: The book that explained why small groups rule large ones. T1: MANCUR OLSON JR (1932-1998) was a North Dakota farm boy who earned a PhD at Harvard and taught for most of his career at the University of Maryland. In 1965 Harvard University Press published his dissertation as THE LOGIC OF COLLECTIVE ACTION: PUBLIC GOODS AND THE THEORY OF GROUPS. T2: Olson's PARADOX: conventional wisdom held that large groups with shared interests would EASILY organize to advance those interests. Olson showed the opposite. In LARGE groups, no individual member has enough at stake to bear the costs of organizing -- so large diffuse groups typically FAIL to organize. T3: the mechanism is FREE-RIDING. If ten million taxpayers each stand to save $10 by defeating a subsidy, no individual taxpayer has enough at stake to spend a weekend organizing opposition. But if a hundred beneficiaries each stand to GAIN $1,000,000 from the same subsidy, each of them has enough at stake to hire lobbyists, contribute to campaigns, and monitor legislation full-time. T4: the CONCENTRATED-BENEFITS / DISPERSED-COSTS PATTERN: policies with concentrated beneficiaries and dispersed victims TEND TO PASS AND SURVIVE, even when the total social cost exceeds the total social benefit. The beneficiaries organize; the victims do not. This is the STRUCTURAL EXPLANATION for the survival of farm subsidies, sugar tariffs, occupational licensing, and thousands of other policies that persist despite failing any cost-benefit test. T5: Olson's book was RECOGNIZED across disciplines. Political scientists adopted it as basic theory; sociologists used it to explain social-movement failure; economists slotted it into public choice. Olson himself extended the analysis in THE RISE AND DECLINE OF NATIONS (1982, Yale University Press) -- the second of his three great books -- and in POWER AND PROSPERITY (2000, posthumous). Further rungs: SELECTIVE INCENTIVES (private benefits that only members receive) are Olson's answer to how any large group DOES manage to organize -- unions offer contracts, professional associations offer certifications, AARP offers insurance discounts; the AARP membership card is a textbook Olson example.

name: Applied Olson: farm subsidies, sugar tariffs, occupational licensing

T2: the math: a large commercial farm may receive $100,000+ per year in direct payments, crop insurance subsidies, and price supports. A typical taxpayer household pays perhaps $80 per year to fund the whole program. Farmers organize (Farm Bureau, National Cotton Council, corn-growers' association); taxpayers do not. Farm-state senators trade votes; consumer-state senators shrug. The system SURVIVES every decade because Olson's structural math holds. T3: the US SUGAR PROGRAM is even purer. Tariff-rate quotas and price supports raise US sugar prices to roughly TWICE world prices. About 4,000 US sugar producers (heavily concentrated in Florida, Louisiana, and North Dakota) capture roughly $1 billion in extra revenue per year. Roughly 330 million American consumers pay an extra ~$3 each per year in higher prices for anything sweetened. Try organizing 330 million people to save $3 each. T4: OCCUPATIONAL LICENSING is the same math applied to labor markets. In 1950, roughly 5% of US workers needed a state license to do their jobs. name: The Rise and Decline of Nations 1982
scope: Olson's macro-history extension of the collective-action theory. T1: in 1982, YALE UNIVERSITY PRESS published MANCUR OLSON'S THE RISE AND DECLINE OF NATIONS: ECONOMIC GROWTH, STAGFLATION, AND SOCIAL RIGIDITIES. It applied the LOGIC of collective action to comparative economic history at national scale. T2: the CENTRAL THESIS: in stable, peaceful societies, DISTRIBUTIONAL COALITIONS (interest groups, cartels, unions, licensing guilds, subsidy recipients) accumulate over time. Each new coalition secures small privileges for its members at the expense of the general economy. Eventually the accumulated weight of these coalitions STRANGLES economic growth. T3: the counterintuitive prediction: societies that experience MAJOR SHOCKS -- wars, revolutions, occupations -- often GROW FASTER afterwards because those shocks DESTROY the accumulated distributional coalitions. Postwar economies get a FRESH START without the encrusted layers of interest-group privilege. T4: Olson's EMPIRICAL CASES: postwar WEST GERMANY and JAPAN both grew dramatically faster than the victorious UNITED STATES and BRITAIN in the 1950s and 1960s. Why? Because the war had DESTROYED their old industrial cartels, unions, and licensing guilds -- allowing rebuilt economies to start with fresh rules. Britain, which had accumulated distributional coalitions since the Industrial Revolution without a similar shock, suffered relative decline. T5: this is why REFORM is so hard in old democracies -- every distributional coalition fights fiercely to preserve its privileges, and no cross-society organized force fights BACK. Olson called this the STRUCTURAL EXPLANATION for the productivity slowdowns of the 1970s. His theory does NOT predict inevitable decline -- societies can consciously dismantle distributional coalitions (Britain 1979-90 under Thatcher; New Zealand 1984-88 under Roger Douglas) and restore growth. But left alone, entrenched interests win. Further rungs: The Rise and Decline of Nations won the AMERICAN POLITICAL SCIENCE ASSOCIATION'S GLADYS M. KAMMERER AWARD; Olson pointedly compared US Southern-state economic revival after the Civil War disruption to the sluggishness of the industrialized Northeast.

name: William Niskanen: bureaucrats maximize budgets
scope: The book that applied public-choice reasoning to bureaucracy. T1: WILLIAM NISKANEN (1933-2011) was a Chicago-trained economist who served as director of economics at the Ford Motor Company, then in the Nixon-era Office of Management and Budget, and later chairman of Reagan's Council of Economic Advisers (1981-85). From 1985 until his death he chaired the CATO INSTITUTE. T2: in 1971 he published BUREAUCRACY AND REPRESENTATIVE GOVERNMENT (Aldine-Atherton) -- a slim volume that applied economic reasoning to bureaucratic incentives. T3: the CENTRAL MOVE: what do bureaucrats MAXIMIZE? Neoclassical welfare economics had implicitly assumed they maximize 'public welfare' or 'agency mission.' Niskanen argued they maximize what actually accrues to THEM PERSONALLY: SALARY, PRESTIGE, STAFF SIZE, PERQUISITES, AGENCY POWER, and PROMOTION PROSPECTS. All of these are POSITIVELY CORRELATED with AGENCY BUDGET. T4: therefore: bureaucrats FIGHT FOR BIGGER BUDGETS. Not because they are wicked; because their entire career incentive structure rewards budget growth. Whatever their agency's official mission, its INCENTIVE-COMPATIBLE behavior is to expand -- to increase staff, to expand scope, to defend turf against rival agencies, to justify budget increases through crisis and mission creep. T5: this predicts several observed patterns: agencies rarely conclude that their mission is 'done'; agencies grow during their host administration's terms and rarely shrink under opposition administrations (Reagan's administration cut a few agency budgets modestly, but total federal employment BARELY MOVED); agencies with unclear performance metrics grow fastest because failure cannot be measured. The Niskanen model is FRIENDLY to public choice's larger project -- it shows that assuming bureaucratic benevolence leads to systematically wrong predictions. Further rungs: Niskanen resigned from Reagan's CEA over the administration's fiscal deficits and its abandonment of a serious spending-cut agenda; the Niskanen-model of bureau behavior was extended by ANTHONY DOWNS in Inside Bureaucracy (1967) with a typology of bureaucratic personality types (climbers, conservers, zealots, advocates, statesmen).

name: Anthony Downs and the median-voter theorem
scope: The book that founded formal public-choice modeling of elections. T1: in 1957, HARPER & BROTHERS published ANTHONY DOWNS'S AN ECONOMIC THEORY OF DEMOCRACY -- Downs's dissertation under Kenneth Arrow at Stanford. It applied economic modeling to voting for the first time. T2: the SETUP: model voters as self-interested actors who vote for the party whose platform best serves their interests, and model parties as vote-maximizing entities that adjust platforms to attract voters. Where do platforms end up? T3: the MEDIAN VOTER THEOREM: under simple-majority voting on a single issue with voter preferences arrayed on a spectrum (say, tax rates from 0% to 100%), the winning platform CONVERGES TO the preference of the MEDIAN VOTER -- the voter whose preference is exactly in the middle of the distribution. Duncan Black had proved the mathematical version in 1948; Downs popularized it and applied it to political competition. T4: the reasoning: if the median voter wants a 30% tax rate and Party A proposes 35% while Party B proposes 20%, Party B can INCREASE its vote share by moving its platform right up to 29% -- capturing every voter left of the midpoint between the platforms. Party A then moves toward the median in defense. Both parties converge on the median voter's preference. This explains why the two major American parties on many issues look SIMILAR AT ELECTION TIME. T5: Downs also introduced RATIONAL IGNORANCE. Studying candidates and issues costs time. The expected influence of any individual vote on the outcome is essentially zero. Therefore, RATIONAL VOTERS MINIMIZE the time they spend informing themselves about politics -- most voters remain fundamentally uninformed about most policy questions, not because they are stupid but because it is RATIONAL to remain ignorant given the near-zero return on voting-relevant investment. Further rungs: Downs later worked in urban economics and traffic planning (his 'law of peak-hour expressway congestion' is standard reference); the median-voter theorem has known LIMITATIONS -- it assumes single-peaked preferences and one-dimensional issue spaces (Arrow's Impossibility Theorem shows multidimensional cases can lack a stable equilibrium).

T3: Caplan identified FOUR SYSTEMATIC BIASES that ECONOMISTS have across the ideological spectrum but VOTERS do not: (1) ANTI-MARKET BIAS (voters underestimate the benefits of the market mechanism); (2) ANTI-FOREIGN BIAS (voters underestimate the benefits of trade with other countries); (3) MAKE-WORK BIAS (voters value jobs for their own sake, not what jobs PRODUCE); (4) PESSIMISTIC BIAS (voters systematically overestimate how bad economic conditions are and how much worse things are getting). name: Kenneth Arrow's Impossibility Theorem 1951
scope: The mathematical result that broke 'the will of the people' as a coherent concept. T1: KENNETH ARROW (1921-2017) was a Columbia-and-Chicago-trained mathematical economist who won the 1972 NOBEL PRIZE in economic sciences at age 51 -- the YOUNGEST economics Nobel to that date. His doctoral dissertation at Columbia (1951) became SOCIAL CHOICE AND INDIVIDUAL VALUES (Wiley 1951). T2: the QUESTION he asked: is there any VOTING SYSTEM (or more generally, any method for aggregating individual preferences into a group preference) that satisfies a short list of REASONABLE FAIRNESS CRITERIA simultaneously? Criteria like: if every voter prefers A to B, the group prefers A to B; irrelevant alternatives should not flip the ranking; no single voter should be a dictator. T3: Arrow's THEOREM: no such method exists. For any group of three or more voters facing three or more choices, EVERY conceivable aggregation method violates at least one of the reasonable criteria. It is a MATHEMATICAL IMPOSSIBILITY. T4: the CONSEQUENCE for democracy: there is NO WELL-DEFINED 'WILL OF THE PEOPLE' independent of the voting method used to elicit it. Different methods (majority rule, Borda count, instant-runoff, approval voting) produce DIFFERENT WINNERS from the same voter preferences. Which method you choose determines the outcome AS MUCH AS the voters do. T5: this DEEPENS public choice's institutional-focus. If there is no coherent 'people's will' waiting to be discovered, then the specific INSTITUTIONS (the voting method, the agenda-setting rules, the committee structures) MATTER ENORMOUSLY -- because they DETERMINE the outcome. Buchanan's constitutional political economy takes on additional weight: RULES are not merely constraints on the aggregation of preferences; they PARTLY DEFINE what 'the aggregate preference' even is. Further rungs: DUNCAN BLACK's median-voter theorem (1948) is the KNOWN EXCEPTION -- if voter preferences are single-peaked on a single issue dimension, majority rule DOES produce a stable outcome (the median voter). Arrow's Theorem shows the exception is narrow.

name: Bootleggers and Baptists: Bruce Yandle 1983
scope: The coalition pattern that explains why odd regulations survive. T3: the SIGNATURE example is Sunday liquor bans in Southern states. BAPTISTS supported the bans on MORAL GROUNDS -- alcohol was sinful and Sunday should be observed. Together they were more effective politically than either alone -- the Baptists gave the regulation MORAL COVER; the bootleggers provided quiet financial support. T5: the reasoning-move: whenever a regulation has an obvious MORAL JUSTIFICATION and simultaneously has quiet SUPPORT from parties who would PROFIT from the restriction, expect the moral coalition to be doing the visible lobbying while the profit coalition supplies the resources. name: Ronald Coase: transaction costs and social cost
scope: The economist who showed that externalities can often be solved by private bargaining. T1: RONALD COASE (1910-2013) was an English-born economist who spent most of his career at the University of Chicago Law School. He won the 1991 NOBEL PRIZE in economic sciences 'for his discovery and clarification of the significance of transaction costs and property rights for the institutional structure and functioning of the economy.' T2: his first great paper was 'THE NATURE OF THE FIRM' (Economica 1937), written when Coase was 27. Its question: why do FIRMS exist at all? If markets are so good at coordinating economic activity, why do we not use markets for everything -- hiring an accountant for the day when we need accounting, contracting with a delivery driver for each package, etc.? T3: his answer: because MARKET TRANSACTIONS have COSTS -- finding partners, negotiating contracts, monitoring performance, enforcing agreements. Firms exist to REPLACE some market transactions with in-house command relationships (a manager tells an employee what to do rather than negotiating a new contract every hour). The firm's size is determined by where in-house costs equal transaction costs. This founded TRANSACTION COST ECONOMICS. T4: his second great paper was 'THE PROBLEM OF SOCIAL COST' (Journal of Law and Economics 1960). Its argument transformed the economics of externalities. Standard Pigou-style analysis: if a factory pollutes and harms a neighbor, the state should tax the pollution to internalize the externality. Coase pointed out that IF TRANSACTION COSTS ARE LOW, the factory and the neighbor could BARGAIN to an efficient outcome -- whichever party is harmed less would compensate the other. T5: the COASE THEOREM -- when transaction costs are LOW enough that parties can negotiate, PROPERTY RIGHTS (whoever holds the initial legal right) determine WHO PAYS in the bargain, but the FINAL ALLOCATION is EFFICIENT regardless of which party held the initial right. When transaction costs are HIGH (many affected parties, unclear boundaries, prohibitive negotiation), Coase's analysis DOES support government intervention -- but the government analysis must include the transaction costs of the government solution too, not compare private cost to zero-cost idealized state action. Further rungs: Coase's 1960 paper is one of the MOST-CITED economics papers ever; he was 100 years old when he published his last book HOW CHINA BECAME CAPITALIST (with Ning Wang, 2012) -- he was 102 when he died in 2013.

name: Elinor Ostrom: Governing the Commons 1990
scope: The first-woman-Nobel-in-economics who showed the commons could self-govern. T1: ELINOR OSTROM (1933-2012) was an INDIANA UNIVERSITY political scientist who won the 2009 NOBEL MEMORIAL PRIZE IN ECONOMIC SCIENCES 'for her analysis of economic governance, especially the commons' -- the FIRST WOMAN ever to win the economics Nobel. It attacked a widely-held academic assumption: that COMMON-POOL RESOURCES (fisheries, grazing lands, irrigation systems, forests) INEVITABLY suffered the TRAGEDY OF THE COMMONS as popularized in Garrett Hardin's 1968 Science paper -- absent state or market intervention. T3: Ostrom's EMPIRICAL CASE studies documented DOZENS of real-world commons that had been successfully self-governed by their users for CENTURIES without state ownership OR privatization. Examples: Swiss ALPINE PASTURES (grazing rules established medieval, still enforced), JAPANESE VILLAGE COMMONS (iriaichi forestry systems), MAINE LOBSTER FISHERIES (informal territorial boundaries enforced by local lobstermen), NEPALESE IRRIGATION SYSTEMS (rotating water-allocation rules maintained by cultivators). T4: her EIGHT DESIGN PRINCIPLES for successful commons self-governance: (1) clearly defined boundaries; (2) rules matched to local conditions; (3) collective-choice arrangements; (4) monitoring; (5) graduated sanctions; (6) low-cost conflict resolution; (7) minimal recognition of self-organization by external authorities; (8) nested enterprises for large systems. These design principles were EMPIRICALLY DERIVED from her comparative case-study work, not deduced from theory. T5: Ostrom's contribution to the public-choice tradition: she added a THIRD option to the state-vs-market binary that had dominated the debate. Commons could be governed successfully by NEITHER the state NOR the market -- by SELF-ORGANIZED USER GROUPS with the right institutional design. name: Vincent Ostrom: polycentric political systems
scope: The husband-half of the Bloomington School and its constitutional political-economy branch. T1: VINCENT OSTROM (1919-2012) was a UCLA-trained political scientist who spent his career at INDIANA UNIVERSITY (1964-2012). With his wife ELINOR OSTROM, he co-founded the WORKSHOP IN POLITICAL THEORY AND POLICY ANALYSIS in 1973 -- the institutional home of what would become known as the BLOOMINGTON SCHOOL. T2: Ostrom's foundational contribution was the concept of POLYCENTRIC POLITICAL SYSTEMS -- systems in which MULTIPLE overlapping decision-making centers each have some autonomous authority, rather than a single centralized hierarchy. He developed this in a 1961 paper with CHARLES TIEBOUT and ROBERT WARREN, 'THE ORGANIZATION OF GOVERNMENT IN METROPOLITAN AREAS' (American Political Science Review 1961). T3: their argument attacked the METROPOLITAN CONSOLIDATION movement of the 1950s, which had held that fragmented local governments in American metropolitan areas (thousands of cities, school districts, water districts) were inefficient and should be MERGED into unified metropolitan governments. Ostrom + Tiebout + Warren showed empirically that FRAGMENTED SYSTEMS often PERFORMED BETTER than consolidated ones -- with more responsive service delivery, more experimentation, and more citizen exit-and-voice options. T4: his 1971 book POLITICAL THEORY OF A COMPOUND REPUBLIC applied polycentric analysis to the AMERICAN FOUNDING. Ostrom argued that the Founders' choice of FEDERALISM -- multiple layers of government with separately-derived authorities -- was itself a polycentric institutional design, chosen deliberately over the alternative of unified national government. The FEDERALIST PAPERS (Publius) were Ostrom's core primary sources. T5: Ostrom's LATER WORK -- MEANING OF AMERICAN FEDERALISM (1991), MEANING OF DEMOCRACY AND THE VULNERABILITY OF DEMOCRACIES (1997) -- warned that CENTRALIZATION in American governance during the twentieth century (New Deal, Great Society, post-9/11 security state) was ERODING the polycentric constitutional structure the Founders designed. His 1997 book was a Tocquevillean warning that democracies whose polycentric structure is dismantled become vulnerable to collapse. Vincent Ostrom died June 29 2012 -- FOUR WEEKS after his wife Elinor. Further rungs: the 1961 Tiebout-Warren-Ostrom paper is one of the most-cited public-administration papers ever; the Bloomington School continues at Indiana as the Ostrom Workshop.
